content:
I'm a beginner in Lean, coming from more mainstream industry programming languages, and still relatively new to type theory, ML style functional programming, and constructive mathematics. I've been learning Lean and trying it out for practical programs, and it seems like there is large use-case overlap between these different constructs in the language

Let's take the case of representing a coordinate or force in 3D space, a physics vector. I see 4 reasonable ways of representing this:
1) Tuples ℝ × ℝ × ℝ
2) Structures structure Vector3 where (x y z : ℝ)
3) Length indexed Vectors Vector ℝ 3
4) Length refined Lists { l : List ℝ // l.length = 3 }

Most of the trade-offs appear to in cosmetics and ergonomics.
My thoughts so far,

tuples:

  • immediately strikes me as the most direct and familiar notation, elegant and easy to write, both as a type ascription and for instantiating them.
  • Must write .1 .2.1 .2.2 instead of .x, .y, .z, there appear to be no named tuples in this language like Scala offers.
  • Even if I define .x, .y, .z aliases, I can't use them in {position with x := ... update notation.

structures:

  • has named .x, .y, .z fields.
  • can use with notation on those fields.
  • requires first defining the structure before you can use it as a type, which is fine in the case of coordinates, but worse in others (I would rather do WIndow.size : (w h : ℝ) than needing to go make a structure Size and write size : Size)
  • is worse to read in my opinion, seeing the shape of types is often better than seeing an english word.

Then on Length-indexed Vectors vs refined List subtypes, I question the purpose of Vectors. The ability to refine Lists by size seems to make Vectors obsolete, but subtypes simply look more painful to work regarding language support for them, so Vector seems like an workaround for that?

I would like to hear any advice or other features of these constructs I might be missing for how I should go about choosing the right one in scenarios. Any corrections on mistakes I've made are appreciated. Thanks.
For physics vectors I suggest using Fin n -> \R
if you want to compute, use docs#Vector
Ultimately the answer depends on what you wish to express and what you wish to use the object for

There is actually another option, which you might want to consider. Mathlib tends to use Fin 3 -> ℝ (nicknamed FinVec) for three-dimensional vectors, or n -> ℝ where {n : Type*} [Fintype n] for n-dimensional vectors. See e.g. the code around docs#Matrix.vecMul for basic examples of how this works in practice.

With these vectors, you can access the entries as v 0 v 1 v 2 (given v : Fin 3 -> ℝ), update them with docs#Function.update, and construct them with the ![a, b, c] notation. Drawback is that the functions are not very efficient computation-wise, since every time you evaluate (v + w) 0 it recomputes v 0 + w 0.

This is also my suggestion. Fwiw, when I was writing my vector linear search and binary search, I first started with Fin vecs. There seems to be some missing API for FinVec around take and drop as well. simp was able to find me the corresponding versions of docs#Vector, so I went ahead with that.
What would be the advantages of using FinVec over a tuple or structure or Vector ℝ 3?
integration with matrices for example?
I see. Well, in my case I'm not trying to do theorem proving, rather am intending to run applications, using Lean as a practical functional programming language. So I will compute these.
Then docs#Vector is the better choice.
Yes, Vector is good for computation, but I'd probably go for a specialized structure in this case.

Jovan Gerbscheid said:

but I'd probably go for a specialized structure in this case.

Could you go on a bit about why? I also have some intuition about which constructs to use in certain situations, structure seems more familiar coming from how I would do this in OOP, but I would really like to have more concrete heuristics about why people choose each construct in each situation. When I personally try to analyze it, I just come up with trade-offs in ergonomics and cosmetics, and that feels arbitrary.
We could help better with a concrete example I guess

This is the real example I ran into, I'm playing around with coding a video game in Lean, so I needed to represent 3D vectors and do operations on them for representing positions, velocities and forces for entities.
You would be better off with 3D vectors (for positions and such) or 4D vectors (quaternions). The underlying API has many parts implemented in C. You need performance for video game stuff.
I am referring to docs#Vector of course.
You might want to check this repository : https://github.com/Kiiyya/lean-wgpu

What's your reasoning in favor of Vector over a structure? One disadvantage I see is that with Vectors the access notation looks a bit awkward compared to what you would typically see in a video game engine api, whereas with structure then game logic code can mention .x, .y, .z
Performance.
Vector is a thin wrapper around Array, and the (actual) implementation of Array (that runs when you execute Vector stuff) is C code or very efficient but unsafe lean code.

I don't think there's a noticable performance difference; both Array and a custom structure have almost the same runtime representation (in fact a structure will be smaller due to not storing size and capacity); and both structures and arrays have efficient lookup functions that end up just being one pointer dereference (with an offset). Also, a structure has the potential to be unboxed eventually while Arrays are probably going to stay on the heap for a while.
So if performance is the metric, structures are the better one (but probably not by much).
Wouldn’t arrays also join the list of things that we can eventually have unboxed? Haskell has unboxed arrays

structure is the fastest here, faster than Vector. With a structure, the compiler knows that the thing has exactly 3 elements. With a Vector, this information exists only in the type, but the compiler erases types.

@Shreyas Srinivas, maybe you are thinking of docs#ByteArray. This acts like an unboxed array of UInt8, and you can use unsafeCast if you want to store specific other types. But using that will make your life more difficult.

I wouldn't completely exclude the possibility of having unboxed arrays but the dynamic size of arrays definitely makes it harder to work with them on the stack. For structures it's much more obvious how you work with them on the stack (i.e. just like a C struct)
Vector is statically sized though
The compiler doesn't know that though
We could specialize vectors to use an unboxed version for implementation purposes couldn't we?
That sounds really hard. How would we compile polymorphic code then?

This is of course going a bit into the hypothetical. The most recent message I found from the FRO side suggests that we still don't have unboxed structures : #lean4 dev > Unboxed structure types @ 💬

But I would expect that for performance we would only need to specialize for Int (sized) and Float types. Other vector types could run boxed.

The specific issue here appears to be numerical calculations on vectors, and these are fairly common as we know (numerical linear algebra and all that), but mostly for ints and floats. Inventing a new structure everytime we want a different dimension of vectors seems inconvenient.
You can use ByteArray to represent such data.
ByteArray packs everything into UInt8. That packing and unpacking has linear time
Yes, you would do your expensive computations on ByteArray itself. There is no need to unpack and repack every time.

Anyway, for this topic, if structures are best and they already exist in unpacked form, then that's probably the answer. I do think an RFC for adding specialized unboxed treatment of Vector Int64 n and Vector Float n would be awesome to have.
